extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors (elementary through undergraduate), discrete math / algebra / precalculus teachers, teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_description: Classroom-tested projects/worksheets for teaching discrete-mathematics topics (pile-splitting/strong induction, multinomial/Euler triangles, and a combinatorics/logic coloring game). Each project includes instructor notes, student worksheets, hands-on suggestions, and extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjecture and prove general solution using strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Worksheet asks students to play the pile-splitting puzzle, conjecture the formula for the sum of products, and prove the conjecture correct using the strong form of the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students play with examples to observe patterns, then use a strong-induction proof. The worksheet includes a complete proof for one variant to model the technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manipulatives / hands-on exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students with beads or pennies so each student can actively play the pile-splitting game for several n to see patterns emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students who discover the conjecture can assist others; hands-on exploration is recommended before formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present and require a template/script for induction proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: During the induction phase present a template or 'script' for a correct induction argument and require students to follow it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice builds confidence and logical understanding of how induction works; the Worksheet includes a complete proof example to use as a script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign variants and extensions as follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: After presenting the main puzzle and proof, give students additional variants (e.g., different computed quantities at each split) to conjecture and prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants both in-class and as homework deepen understanding; examples and solutions (e.g., sum = n and n-1 for two variants) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect puzzle to recursion and recurrence relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the recursive nature of pile-splitting to discuss recursive definitions, recurrence relations, solving recurrences, and recursive algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how a recursive algorithm's correctness can be justified by strong induction; tie to techniques students will learn for linear recurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete sequence data to identify formula and recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute small n examples, form sequence of sums, examine differences and recurrences to conjecture closed form (e.g., an = (n^3 - n)/3 or (n^2 - n)/2 depending on variant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This empirical approach can lead to the same solution without induction, but is useful pedagogically before introducing formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate student level and time allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing Pascal (Euler triangles) activity: appropriate for mature Algebra and Precalculus students; can be completed in two or three one-hour class periods depending on background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit this unit after a binomial expansion unit; adjust depth for audience and time available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pegboard/templates/strings for path-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students string or draw paths on an Euler-triangle template (trinomial/quadrinomial, etc.) to count paths that produce multinomial coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical templates or pegboards make the counting-paths method tangible (examples and photos provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach recursive construction of Euler triangle entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute each non-initial entry by summing the m entries that are adjacent and above it (two for binomial, three for trinomial, etc.), with base/edge rules for indices out of range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce Euler's notation for multinomial coefficients; present recursive definition explicitly and illustrate with examples (Figures included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and prove structural properties (symmetry, row length, row sums, diagonals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead students to discover: triangle rows are palindromic (symmetric), each new row has m-1 more entries for an m-nomial, row sum equals m^n, and certain diagonals contain figurate numbers (e.g., triangular numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counting arguments and algebraic substitution (set x=1) to justify row-sum claims; exercises prompt students to formalize these observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CAS to verify expansions when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage using a Computer Algebra System (e.g., DERIVE) to expand (1 + x + x^2 + ...)^n and check computed coefficients for larger examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAS can speed verification for students once they understand the combinatorial construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide progressive exercises toward generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises ask students to build trinomial/quadrinomial/quintinomial triangles, find next rows, compute expansions, and generalize to m-nomials (including closed forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks a–f that escalate: create rows, compute sums, derive closed forms, and prove general row-sum = m^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pose research-level questions as extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest open or deeper questions: find closed form for trinomial coefficients, closed form for general m-nomial coefficients, and explain why certain diagonals equal known figurate numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provide opportunities for projects or advanced student investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt activity to multiple grade levels and course contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Coloring-and-rectangles project is suitable for elementary, middle, high school, undergraduate, and graduate teacher-education courses, with complexity scaled to level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler board sizes and guided questions for younger students; use combinatorics/symmetry/logic extensions for older students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use game-like reveal/guess mechanic to develop inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor pre-colors a board partitioned into four rectangular regions (one rectangle per color). Students ask for the color of one square at a time and infer other squares ('freebies') using geometry and logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective is to determine the full coloring in as few guesses as possible; teach students to choose guesses that reveal maximal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote cooperative learning and mathematical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend students work in groups and finish with whole-class discussion; require explanations of reasoning to foster communication skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many acceptable solutions exist for some problems, group work reduces grading load and supports dialogical learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design board and representation details explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor should color a (10 x 10) board (example) with four rectangular regions of integer dimensions; colors may be represented by suits (♠, ♥, ♦, ♣) and coordinates use matrix (row,column) notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any rectangular board size will suffice; the 10 x 10 is a convenient example used in the worksheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify configurations up to symmetry and count cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead students to discover equivalence classes of rectangle-partitions (six configuration classes if rotation/reflection and rectangle sizes are disregarded) and use these to count total colorings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (3–6) guide students to partitioning decisions that force configuration class; use symmetry to reduce counting complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate minimal-information and enumeration problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems ask students to determine minimal numbers of revealed squares needed to deduce full coloring, to compute best next guess strategies, and to count the total number of valid colorings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine logical deduction with combinatorics and symmetry to answer these optimization and enumeration tasks; worksheet includes sample boards and counting prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan grading and logistics given multiple acceptable answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Worksheet notes that because many acceptable answers exist for some problems, grading many individual submissions can be tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider group submissions or in-class discussion to reduce grading burden and emphasize reasoning over single numeric answers.
